name: Highlighter

lead: A highlighter is a cosmetic that reflects light. Placed on the high points of the face, such as the cheekbones and the bone beneath the eyebrow, it makes those areas look brighter and more prominent, which creates a sense of depth and shape. It is often used together with contour shading, which does the opposite on the hollows.

Theatre and film performers used it first, to define cheekbones, nose and jawline when filming indoors without natural light, and it reached everyday consumers later, with social media tutorials and selfies credited by some industry experts for a sales jump around 2016. No clinical studies have examined it; its use is documented through makeup practice.

paras: It comes as powder, liquid, cream, gloss, stick or jelly, usually in white or champagne tones, with colored versions for particular looks. People apply it to the cheekbones, the outer brow bone and similar high points, often over foundation and next to contour. It lasts for the day it is worn and is removed with normal makeup removal.

Risks are those of cosmetics in general: skin irritation or allergy to an ingredient, and breakouts for some skin types. Glitter or shimmer particles near the eyes can be uncomfortable. Some people find the effect looks different in flash photography or bright light.

angle.text: Applied to the high points of the face, highlighter makes them reflect light, so cheekbones and the brow area look more prominent and the face appears to have more depth. The effect lasts as long as the makeup is worn.

lead: A highlighter is a light-reflecting cosmetic used to brighten an area of skin and suggest depth or angles; it is often paired with contouring.[1][2] Placed on the cheekbones and the outer brow bone, it makes those high points catch light, so the face reads as more defined and sculpted while the makeup is worn.[1]

Highlighters come as powders, liquids, creams, glosses, solid sticks and jellies, usually in white or champagne shades, with blue, pink and rainbow versions for particular looks.[1] In contouring routines a darker shade is placed in the hollows of the cheeks, beside the nose and on the temples, a lighter highlighter goes on prominent areas such as the cheekbone apples, nose tip and T-zone, and the lighter-only approach is called strobing.[2]

The product grew out of stage and film makeup, where performers relied on shading and highlighting to define features under artificial light. MAC Cosmetics' Strobing Cream is credited as the first highlighter sold to everyday consumers, and sales rose sharply in 2016, which some industry experts link to YouTube tutorials and selfies.[1] No clinical studies have examined cosmetic highlighter.

paras: Highlighters come as powders, liquids, creams, glosses, sticks and jellies; usual shades are white or champagne, with some in blue, pink or rainbow colors for particular makeup looks.[1] Powder contour products are often sold in light-and-dark palettes, while cream products give a more emphasized look.[2]
The word 'highlighter' also names the fluorescent marker pen for text; the cosmetic sense is a separate, later usage.[3]

The effect is optical. Light-reflecting product on a high point makes that spot look closer to the light and more prominent, while shade in a hollow recedes, so a flat-looking face gains planes. Makeup artists describe this as suggesting depth and angles.[2] Applied to the cheekbones it makes them look higher and more pronounced, and on the outer brow bone it lifts the eye area.[1]

In looksmaxxing discussions, makeup of this kind is raised as a temporary way to emphasize cheekbones, a jawline or the brow area, for photos or dates; related practices are covered in the entries on cheekbone and jaw contouring makeup. The effect lasts as long as the makeup is worn and is removed with ordinary makeup removal.

Theatre and film actors used highlighter when working indoors, where natural light could not define features such as the cheekbones, nose and jawline; it also let them emphasize or downplay features to suit a character or current trend.[1]

The wider tradition of contouring is traced by Wikipedia to Elizabethan stage actors, who used chalk and soot so audiences could read their expressions, and to the late 1800s, when electric stage lighting led to greasepaint replacing soot. Marlene Dietrich used shading and sculpting on film in the 1920s and 1930s, and makeup artist Max Factor Sr. added shading so faces would not look flat on film, reportedly giving the first face-shape contouring tutorial in 1945.[2] Actresses such as Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe and Elizabeth Taylor wore subtle contouring in the 1950s.[2]

Makeup artist Kevyn Aucoin shaped the sculpted look of many celebrities, and his 2000 book Face Forward is credited with introducing contouring to the general public.[2] In the 2010s Kim Kardashian and makeup artists popularized the technique, and brands began selling dedicated contour and strobing products.[2] MAC Cosmetics' Strobing Cream is credited as the first highlighter sold to consumers, and sales rose significantly in 2016, which experts linked partly to social media, including YouTube makeup tutorials and selfies.[1] Drag performers also use contour and highlight to emphasize feminine features and soften masculine ones.[2]

It is applied over foundation to the cheekbones, outer brow bone and similar high points, often beside contour shade.[1][2] Contouring is also used on other parts of the body, which gained attention through celebrity images on social media in the 2000s.[2]

Risks are those of cosmetics generally: skin irritation or allergy to an ingredient, and breakouts for some skin types. Shimmer particles near the eyes can be uncomfortable, and the effect can look different in flash photography or bright light.

lore.intro: Highlighter is discussed in makeup and looks communities as a quick, reversible way to make cheekbones and the brow area look more prominent.[1][2]
